主要内容: The U.S. Treasury announced sanctions against Iran on February 6, 2013, as part of the Iran Threat Reduction and Syria Human Rights Act (TRA) of 2012. These measures aim to further restrict Iran’s access to oil revenues and target individuals and entities involved in human rights abuses and censorship. The sanctions expand the scope of sanctionable transactions with the Central Bank of Iran and designated financial institutions, limiting Iran’s ability to repatriate oil revenue held in foreign financial institutions. The Treasury designated one individual and four entities for their involvement in Iran’s censorship activities, including the Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB) and its director, Ezzatollah Zarghami. These designations block U.S. persons from engaging in transactions with the designated entities. The sanctions do not apply to humanitarian trade, such as the sale of agricultural commodities, food, medicine, or medical devices to Iran. The Treasury issued guidance to clarify that such trade is exempt from sanctions. The U.S. Treasury announced sanctions against Iran in February 2013, citing its efforts to suppress dissent through state media and internet censorship. The sanctions targeted individuals and entities involved in restricting free speech and controlling information flow. One key figure, Zarghami, who served as the head of Iran's Islamic Radio and Television Network (IRIB), was sanctioned for authorizing the broadcast of forced confessions of political detainees, including journalist Maziar Bahari. The European Union also imposed sanctions on Zarghami for similar actions. Iran has been actively jamming foreign broadcasts, particularly from the BBC and Voice of America (VOA), since the 2009 presidential election. The Iranian Cyber Police, established in 2009, has been tasked with filtering websites, monitoring online behavior, and blocking content deemed objectionable by the government. The Communications Regulatory Authority (CRA) has enforced internet filtering and lawful intercept requirements for telecommunications companies. Iran Electronics Industries (IEI), previously designated under Executive Order 13382, is involved in jamming and monitoring technologies, contributing to the country's efforts to control information access.
